projects.name: Aegis Planner
projects.tagline: A zero-knowledge personal planner. The server only ever stores ciphertext.
projects.problem: Many online planners keep your plans in a form their servers can read, so a breach or a malicious insider can expose all of it.
projects.design: A password-manager key hierarchy in the browser. PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations derives a key-encryption key from the master password; a random 256-bit data key encrypts the vault with AES-256-GCM and is stored only in wrapped form. The Django backend stores only accounts, access rules and encrypted blobs, and never sees plaintext.
highlights: A password change re-wraps the data key; the vault itself is not re-encrypted.
The master password is checked by unwrapping the key: a wrong one fails the GCM tag check. It never leaves the browser.
Saves carry a revision number. A stale write from a second device gets HTTP 409 instead of silently overwriting newer data.
Strict Content-Security-Policy: no inline script, no eval, frame-ancestors 'none'. The frontend is plain JavaScript with no framework, which keeps the policy enforceable.
Argon2 password hashing, per-IP rate limiting, per-username lockout, invite codes and an admin approval gate.
Installable PWA with an offline cache and queued writes. Web Push reminders carry no task text, since the server never has it in readable form.
projects.verification: 146 Django tests and 556 JavaScript checks, run by GitHub Actions on every push.
projects.limits: Does not protect against a compromised device, a malicious browser extension or a leaked master password. The server also delivers the JavaScript that does the encryption, so a compromised server could deliver altered code; any web-based design shares this limit.

main.alt: Aegis Planner web app, Today view in the dark theme, with the day's plan and a reminder to export a vault backup.

inset.alt: Aegis Planner on a phone, Today view with overdue and scheduled tasks.

steps.d: Your master password goes through PBKDF2 with 600,000 iterations and becomes a key that never leaves the browser.
That key unwraps the data key. The password is never sent, and a wrong one fails the AES-GCM check right here.
The whole vault is encrypted with the data key using AES-256-GCM.
Each save carries the revision it was built on.

outcomes.d: The server stores the ciphertext and raises the revision by one.
Another device saved first. The server answers HTTP 409 and stores nothing, so the newer data stays.

projects.name: Aegis Planner
projects.tagline: An offline, encrypted planner for Windows, in Persian with a Jalali calendar.
projects.problem: Many planners need an account and sync your data to a server. This one has no account, no server and no telemetry: everything stays in one encrypted file on the user's computer, and it was designed for Persian speakers from the start.
projects.design: A PyQt6 application over a single AES-256-GCM vault. A random data key encrypts the vault and is wrapped by a key derived with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations. An optional recovery key wraps the same data key independently.
highlights: Changing the password generates a new data key and re-encrypts the vault and every backup, so the old password stops working everywhere.
Crash-safe storage: atomic writes through a temporary file, fsync and rename, plus automatic encrypted backups with verify and restore.
Right-to-left layout, Jalali calendar with Saturday-first weeks, and Persian natural-language quick add.
Release installers are built from tagged source by a public GitHub Actions workflow and published with SHA-256 checksums. The README explains how to verify an unsigned installer.
projects.verification: 971 pytest tests covering the vault format, corrupted and hostile vault files, the Jalali calendar, recurrence, and every page and dialog across themes.
projects.limits: No network access by default. An optional once-a-day version check reads the public GitHub API and sends nothing about the user.

projects.name: Refinery Risk Monitor
projects.tagline: Live risk scoring, forecasting and root-cause analysis for refinery process units.
projects.problem: Operators need to know which process unit is heading toward trouble, why, and how much to trust the forecast.
projects.design: I led the project from scope to delivery, working with a frontend developer, a data analyst and an ML engineer. I set the system architecture and the ML pipeline design, and I directed the backend, which I built with AI coding tools and reviewed. The FastAPI backend serves ML services over REST, streams live risk over WebSocket, and stores data through SQLAlchemy 2.0 with Alembic migrations.
highlights: Role-based access control (operator, engineer, admin) enforced per endpoint with JWT. Self-registration always creates an operator; only an admin can assign higher roles.
In production mode the service refuses to start with a default SECRET_KEY or a wildcard CORS origin.
P10, P50 and P90 quantile forecasts per unit, so every forecast comes with its uncertainty.
Anomaly detection by an ensemble of Isolation Forest, One-Class SVM and Local Outlier Factor, with SHAP explanations of which sensors drive the risk.
Structured JSON logs with correlation IDs, and separate health, readiness and liveness endpoints.
projects.verification: A live simulator with fault injection drives the system end to end. Automated backend tests have not been written yet.
projects.limits: Runs on simulated plant data. Ingesting a real historian or OPC UA feed is planned.

main.alt: Refinery Risk Monitor dashboard in the dark theme: unit count, average risk, critical alerts, risk trend chart and a P10, P50, P90 forecast.

projects.name: Andarun
projects.tagline: A text-only, invite-only social network designed to run on a domestic network when international internet access is cut.
projects.problem: Many social platforms depend on email or phone verification, third-party CDNs and outside services. When a country's international traffic is cut, these are the first to fail.
projects.design: No email and no outside services: username and password login, and every asset served by the app itself. Membership will be invite-only: each new account needs approval from the member who invited it, and invitations form a traceable tree.

decisions.decision: Custom AbstractBaseUser with username as the login field
decisions.reason: No email dependency. Set before the first migration.

decisions.decision: Usernames limited to [a-z0-9_]{3,20} and stored in lowercase
decisions.reason: Rules out look-alike Arabic and Persian characters, and duplicates that differ only in case.

decisions.decision: SECRET_KEY read from the environment, with no fallback
decisions.reason: The app refuses to start without a real key instead of running with a default.
A missing setting can never expose debug pages in production.

decisions.decision: Planned: invite quota checked under a row lock inside transaction.atomic
decisions.reason: Concurrent requests cannot exceed a member's quota.

decisions.decision: Planned: code collisions retried inside a nested savepoint
decisions.reason: A unique-constraint error does not break the outer transaction.

roadmap.scope: Accounts and invitations, text posts, comments, likes, follows, privacy, feed, search, notifications, Docker deploy
Direct and group messages, then end-to-end encryption

tree.caption: Planned: every account traces back to the member who invited it.

projects.limits: Not released yet, and there is no test suite. It has not been tested under a real shutdown; the design relies on having no outside dependencies.

approach.title: Approach
about: I study computer engineering at Islamic Azad University, West Tehran Branch, and work on backend systems with a focus on application security and data integrity.

I use AI coding tools every day. I decide the architecture and the security requirements, and I review what the tools produce before it goes in. Andarun is the exception: I'm writing all of it by hand, to learn Django properly.

principles.title: Fail closed
principles.text: If the configuration is insecure, the service refuses to start.
principles.evidence: Refinery Risk Monitor and Aegis refuse to start in production with a placeholder secret; Andarun will not start without a secret key at all.

principles.title: Keep the server blind
principles.text: Encrypt on the client wherever possible, so a server breach exposes only ciphertext.
principles.evidence: Aegis Web stores only a salt, a wrapped key and ciphertext. Aegis Desktop has no server at all.

principles.title: Make concurrency explicit
principles.text: Every write path assumes another request may be running at the same time.
principles.evidence: Revision-checked writes that return 409 in Aegis Web, and atomic file replacement with fsync in Aegis Desktop.

principles.title: Prove it in CI
principles.text: For the behavior I claim, I write a test and run it on every push.
principles.evidence: Both Aegis projects run their tests in GitHub Actions, and desktop releases are built from tagged source and published with checksums. Refinery Risk Monitor and Andarun do not have test suites yet.
